threads.thread_goal: Align on scope and approve target chart of accounts for relocation jobs.

messages.text: Kicking off the Standardised Accounting and Move-Cost Tracking for Relocation Jobs project. I have uploaded the first draft of the relocation chart of accounts as A1, based on T1. The draft focuses on separating relocation revenue, direct move costs, and dangerous goods surcharges, without changing the core accounting system structure. Please review with an eye on: 1) which relocation activities need their own accounts or subcategories, 2) how we want to see profitability per job and per service type, and 3) anything that might affect statutory or company policy compliance. Feedback in this thread by tomorrow would be ideal so we can iterate quickly within the 21-day window.

Thanks for sharing A1. First impression: the split between relocation revenue and surcharges looks workable. I like that dangerous goods handling is not buried inside general transport costs. One question: for dangerous goods, do we want separate lines for packing, permits, and storage, or is a single dangerous goods handling cost account enough if we capture detail in the job costing template later via A3 and T3? From a compliance angle, as long as we can show total dangerous goods related spend and link it back to specific jobs, either could work, but more granularity might help during audits.

I went through A1 quickly. I see separate accounts for relocation revenue and direct move costs, but I am not fully sure where to post things like tolls, parking, and ferry charges for a job. Are those meant to go into the general transport cost account, or do we need a specific relocation transport subaccount so we do not mix them with non-relocation work? A short example in A1 would help me avoid misposting when we start using the new structure.

Good point on tolls and similar items. In the current A1 draft, they sit under direct transport costs for relocation, but the description is a bit generic. I suggest we keep a single relocation transport cost account and clarify in the usage rules that tolls, parking, and ferry charges for relocation jobs go there, not in general overhead. That keeps the chart lean while still giving us job-level detail through the costing template later. I can add a worked example to A1 to make this explicit.

On the revenue side in A1, do we need separate lines for domestic relocation, international relocation, and storage, or can we keep one relocation revenue account and tag the difference in the job costing template? I am thinking about how many new accounts we can realistically manage without confusing day to day posting.

If we want clear profitability by service type, I would lean toward separate revenue accounts for at least domestic relocation, international relocation, and storage. That way the monthly financial statements and any segment reporting pick this up directly, without relying only on job-level analysis. We can still keep the number of accounts manageable by not splitting too finely beyond that. For dangerous goods surcharges, I would keep a dedicated revenue account so we can reconcile those against the related costs and show auditors the margin on that activity.

On dangerous goods, I see two options for A1: 1) one consolidated dangerous goods handling cost account, with detail captured in A3, or 2) separate accounts for dangerous goods packing, permits, and storage. Given the 21-day deadline and the constraint not to change the core system structure, I propose we start with a single dangerous goods handling cost account and rely on the job costing template to break down packing, permits, and storage. We can revisit further splits after the first audit cycle if needed.

I am comfortable starting with a single dangerous goods handling cost account in A1, as long as A3 clearly separates packing, permits, and storage at job level. That should still give us enough traceability for statutory checks, especially if we can show the link from the job costing template back to the general ledger postings. We just need to make sure the account description in A1 explicitly mentions dangerous goods related costs only, so nothing else drifts in.

If we keep one relocation transport cost account, can we add a short table in A1 listing examples like fuel, tolls, parking, and ferry charges, and maybe what should not go there, like general office travel? That would help me and others when we are posting quickly at month end.
Yes, that makes sense. I will add an examples table to A1 under the relocation transport cost account, with a short do and do not list. That should reduce mispostings when we are under time pressure.

I am ok with separate revenue accounts for domestic relocation, international relocation, storage, and dangerous goods surcharges in A1. Could we also have a small note on how to handle bundled invoices where storage and relocation are on the same invoice line? I want to avoid splitting differently from others.

For bundled invoices, I suggest we add a rule in A1 that we split revenue based on either the agreed price list or a reasonable allocation key, and document the split in the job costing template. That way the general ledger still reflects the separate revenue accounts, and we have a clear explanation if someone asks later.

One more point on scope: do we want separate accounts for relocation related insurance recoveries and claims expenses, or keep them in general insurance? For job profitability, it might be useful to see relocation specific claims and recoveries, especially for dangerous goods incidents.

Given the project objective and the focus on relocation profitability, I propose we add two accounts in A1: relocation claims expense and relocation insurance recoveries. That keeps them visible without overcomplicating the structure. For dangerous goods incidents, we can flag them in the job costing template and in the supporting documentation, but still post to these relocation specific accounts.

If we add relocation claims expense and insurance recoveries, can we also include a short note in A1 on when to use them versus the general insurance accounts? I sometimes struggle with borderline cases, like small damage write offs.

We can add a simple rule in A1: if the claim relates to a specific relocation job, use the relocation claims expense and insurance recovery accounts; if it is a general policy cost or non job specific item, keep it in the existing insurance accounts. I will draft that wording and share with the group for a quick check.

Before we close this, can we list the relocation activities that will definitely have separate tracking lines in A1: domestic relocation revenue, international relocation revenue, storage revenue, dangerous goods surcharge revenue, relocation transport costs, relocation labour costs, dangerous goods handling costs, relocation claims expense, and relocation insurance recoveries. Everything else stays in existing accounts unless clearly relocation specific and agreed later.

Summarising where we have landed on A1 for the project Standardised Accounting and Move-Cost Tracking for Relocation Jobs: 1) We will use separate revenue accounts for domestic relocation, international relocation, storage, and dangerous goods surcharges. 2) We will use dedicated relocation transport and labour cost accounts, plus a single dangerous goods handling cost account, with further breakdown handled in the job costing template. 3) We will add relocation claims expense and relocation insurance recovery accounts for job specific incidents. 4) Examples and posting rules will be expanded in A1 to cover tolls, parking, bundled invoices, and claims vs general insurance. Unless anyone objects by end of day, we will treat this as approval of the proposed relocation chart of accounts and move ahead with T1 configuration and documentation updates.

threads.thread_goal: Define and finalise the relocation accounting SOP, including handover.

messages.text: I have uploaded the first full draft of the relocation accounting SOP as A2, covering T2 and T12. It maps the flow from job creation through to invoicing, including a draft handover checklist from operations to accounting. It also flags where dangerous goods steps need extra documentation, aligned with the compliance guide in A5. Please review and comment on: 1) whether the posting steps are clear enough for day to day work, 2) if the handover data set from operations is realistic, and 3) any missing checks for dangerous goods jobs.

I have gone through A2. The overall flow from job creation to invoice looks consistent with how operations currently works, but I think we should make the dangerous goods steps more explicit. For example, after the job is flagged as dangerous goods, we should require attaching the relevant certificates and permits before posting any dangerous goods handling costs. That will help us meet the statutory obligations summarised in A5 and make it easier to show evidence to auditors later.

In the handover section of A2, the minimum data set from operations includes job ID, customer, origin, destination, and whether it is dangerous goods. I am not sure if we also need the agreed price or rate card reference at that stage, or if that comes later when we raise the invoice. I usually wait for the invoice request email, so I want to check what the new expectation is.

Good question. For the minimum data set in A2 and T12, I would include either the agreed price or a clear reference to the rate card. That way we can validate the invoice amount against something concrete, rather than relying on email threads. It also helps when we prepare sample financial statements later, because we can trace revenue back to the original agreement more easily.

On the end to end flow in A2, I like the step where we check that all job costs are captured before issuing the final invoice. Could we add a simple checklist there, for example: transport, labour, storage, dangerous goods handling, and any third party charges? That would help me avoid missing items when closing a job.

Agree on making dangerous goods steps more explicit. A2 could require that, for any job marked as dangerous goods, we: 1) confirm the dangerous goods classification from operations, 2) attach the relevant permits and certificates, and 3) record the dangerous goods surcharge and handling costs using the accounts defined in A1. This would align with the controls listed in A5 and make it easier to prepare the audit evidence pack later.

Including the agreed price or rate card reference in the handover makes sense. For the minimum data set in A2, should we also require the planned move date and any storage start date, so we know when to expect costs and revenue to hit the accounts?

Yes, I would add planned move date and storage start date to the minimum data set in A2. That will help with cut off and with the monthly reconciliation checklist later. It also gives us a clear point to chase missing costs if nothing has been posted by a certain date.

I like the idea of a short checklist before final invoicing. Maybe we can align it with the fields in the job costing template A3, so that if a cost type exists in A3, we confirm whether it is present or not for that job before closing. That would keep the SOP and the template in sync.

Yes, linking the checklist to A3 makes it easier to remember. If the template has revenue, labour, transport, storage, dangerous goods costs, and third party charges, we can just tick through those before issuing the final invoice.

One more suggestion for A2: in the handover process from operations, we should define a clear cut off time each day when job data must be sent to accounting. That will help us keep daily postings up to date and reduce end of month rush. For example, operations could send the completed jobs list by 4 pm, and we commit to posting same day where possible.

Agreed. I will update A2 so that the minimum data set from operations includes job ID, customer, origin, destination, dangerous goods flag, agreed price or rate card reference, planned move date, storage start date if relevant, and confirmation that all required documents are attached. We will also define a daily cut off time for the handover. This will complete T12 and make the handover process more predictable.

On the posting flow in A2, I just want to confirm: for storage jobs, we recognise revenue monthly based on the storage period, not all upfront when the job is created, right? The draft mentions monthly billing, but I want to be sure the posting steps reflect that.

Correct, for storage we should recognise revenue over time, typically monthly, based on the storage period. A2 should state that clearly in the storage section: when we receive a storage order, we set up the job, but we only post revenue as each storage period is completed and invoiced. I can help refine that wording so it is unambiguous.

For dangerous goods, A2 should also specify that we keep a log of which jobs had dangerous goods surcharges and related costs, so we can reconcile them later and provide evidence to the external auditor. That log could be part of the pilot issue log A7 or a separate register, but the SOP should at least mention it.

To wrap up, here is the proposed end to end posting flow for relocation jobs in A2: 1) Operations creates the job and sends the minimum data set and documents by the daily cut off time. 2) Accounting sets up the job in the system, flags dangerous goods where applicable, and checks that required permits and certificates are attached. 3) As costs are incurred, we post them to the relocation accounts defined in A1, using the job ID as reference. 4) Before issuing the final invoice, we review the job costing template A3 and confirm that all relevant cost types are captured. 5) For storage, we recognise revenue monthly over the storage period. 6) For dangerous goods, we ensure surcharges and handling costs are recorded and logged for compliance, following A5. If there are no objections by tomorrow, we will treat this as agreement on the posting flow and the minimum data set from operations.

threads.thread_goal: Design and validate the job costing template and reconciliation checklist.

messages.text: I have posted initial versions of the relocation job costing template as A3 and the monthly relocation accounts reconciliation checklist as A4, covering T3 and T4. A3 is structured around the new chart of accounts in A1, with sections for revenue, labour, transport, storage, dangerous goods costs, and third party charges. A4 lists the key relocation related accounts and suggested monthly checks. Please review and comment on whether A3 captures everything we need for job profitability and whether A4 is practical for month end.

Looking at A3, the structure aligns well with A1. One suggestion: for dangerous goods, could we add separate columns for packing, permits, and storage, even if they all roll up to the same general ledger account? That would give us more insight into where the dangerous goods costs are coming from without changing the chart of accounts.

In A3, I am not sure where to put small items like packing materials or protective covers that are not dangerous goods. Should they go under labour, transport, or a separate materials line? A short example row would help.

Good catch. We should add a materials and consumables line in A3 for non dangerous goods packing materials and similar items. That will map to the appropriate relocation cost account in A1 and keep labour and transport clean. I will update the template and include an example row.

On A4, the reconciliation checklist looks thorough, but I am a bit worried about the time it will take each month. For example, the step to reconcile each relocation revenue account to the job costing templates might be heavy. Could we instead reconcile total relocation revenue to a summary of A3 templates for the month, rather than job by job?

I agree that a full job by job reconciliation every month would be too heavy. A4 could require a monthly summary of A3 templates by revenue account, and we reconcile that summary to the general ledger balances. We can then sample a few jobs in detail, especially dangerous goods or high value moves, rather than checking every single one.

For A4, I would also add a specific step to reconcile dangerous goods surcharge revenue and dangerous goods handling costs, using the log we mentioned in the SOP and any entries in A3. That will help us show that surcharges are not being missed or misapplied and that costs are properly captured.

If we use a monthly summary of A3 templates for reconciliation, will there be a standard way to prepare that summary, or do we each do it differently? I would prefer if A4 or A3 included a simple summary tab or instructions.

We can add a summary tab to A3 that automatically aggregates revenue and key cost categories by account for the month. A4 can then reference that summary as the basis for the reconciliation. That should keep the process consistent and reduce manual work.

For the dangerous goods reconciliation step in A4, we should also check that each dangerous goods job has the required certificates and permits attached, as per A2 and A5. That way the reconciliation is not just about numbers but also about documentation completeness.

I like the idea of separate columns in A3 for dangerous goods packing, permits, and storage. It will help us see patterns over time, like if permits are driving most of the cost. As long as the template stays simple to fill in, I am on board.

One more thought on A3: should we include a field for job type, such as domestic, international, storage only, or combined? That would make it easier to filter and analyse profitability by type without relying only on account codes.

Yes, adding a job type field to A3 is a good idea. We can align the options with the revenue accounts in A1: domestic relocation, international relocation, storage, and dangerous goods surcharge as a flag. That will help with analysis and with preparing the sample financial statements later.

To test A3 and A4, I suggest we run them on three recent jobs: one domestic move, one international move, and one dangerous goods job. That will help us see if any fields are missing and whether the reconciliation steps in A4 are realistic. We can log any issues in the pilot issue log A7 so they are visible when we start T10.

I can take the dangerous goods job for testing A3 and A4. I will pay attention to whether the template captures all the extra costs and whether the reconciliation step for dangerous goods surcharges and handling costs is clear.

Based on the feedback, I will update A3 to include: 1) separate columns for dangerous goods packing, permits, and storage, 2) a materials and consumables line, 3) a job type field aligned with A1, and 4) a summary tab for monthly reconciliation. For A4, I will: 1) base revenue reconciliation on the A3 summary rather than job by job, 2) add a specific step for dangerous goods surcharge and handling cost reconciliation, and 3) include a documentation check for dangerous goods certificates and permits. Once updated, we can run the three job tests and adjust if needed.

threads.thread_goal: Plan and debrief the pilot of the new process on selected jobs.

messages.text: We are ready to start the pilot of the new relocation accounting process under T10. For the next few days, we will process at least five jobs using the updated SOP in A2 and the job costing template A3. I have created the Pilot Jobs Issue Log as A7 to capture any problems or questions. Please use this thread to confirm which jobs you will pilot and to share any early observations.

I will take two pilot jobs: one domestic move and one dangerous goods move. I will follow A2 step by step, fill in A3 for each job, and log any issues or unclear points in A7. I will pay particular attention to the dangerous goods documentation and how easy it is to reconcile surcharges and handling costs.

I can pick up two more pilot jobs: one international move and one storage only job. I will use A2 and A3 and note any gaps, especially around storage revenue recognition and the handover data from operations.

I can take one smaller domestic job for the pilot. I will try to follow A2 and fill in A3, but I might need help if I get stuck on the new fields. I will log any confusion in A7 so we can adjust the SOP or the template.

Happy to support on the smaller domestic job. If you run into questions on A3 or the posting steps in A2, just note them in A7 and ping me. It will be useful to see where the instructions are not clear enough.

I will focus on reviewing the postings in the accounting system for the pilot jobs, checking that the accounts from A1 are used correctly and that the data from A3 ties back to the general ledger. I will log any mapping or configuration issues in A7 so we can address them under T5.

First update from the dangerous goods pilot job: following A2, I was able to attach the permits and certificates and record the dangerous goods surcharge and handling costs. However, in the system configuration, the dangerous goods surcharge revenue is still mapped to the general relocation revenue account, not the dedicated surcharge account from A1. I have logged this in A7 as a configuration issue.

Thanks for flagging. That mapping issue falls under T5. I will adjust the category mapping so that dangerous goods surcharge revenue posts to the correct account from A1. Once updated, we should re test that job or a similar one to confirm the fix.

On the storage only pilot job, A2 worked fine for setting up the job and recognising revenue monthly. The only friction was that the handover from operations did not include the storage start date, so I had to chase it by email. I logged this in A7 as a data issue so we can reinforce the minimum data set in T12.

On my smaller domestic pilot job, I managed to fill in most of A3, but I was unsure where to put a small claim write off. I ended up leaving it blank and noted the question in A7. The SOP in A2 mentions relocation claims expense, but I was not confident enough to post it without checking.

For that claim write off, A2 and A1 say that if the claim relates to a specific relocation job, we should use the relocation claims expense account. We can update A3 to include a small section for claims and recoveries so it is more obvious where to record it. I will also add a short example to the SOP to make this clearer.

From the postings review, apart from the dangerous goods surcharge mapping, the other accounts from A1 are working as expected. The main pattern in A7 is missing or incomplete handover data from operations, especially planned move dates and storage start dates. That suggests we need to reinforce T12 and maybe add a simple reminder to the operations team.

On the dangerous goods pilot job, once the mapping is fixed, the process in A2 and A3 should work smoothly. The only other issue I noted in A7 is that it takes a bit of time to gather all the dangerous goods documents. We might want to agree with operations that they attach everything before sending the job to accounting, otherwise we risk delays.

We now have five pilot jobs processed and issues logged in A7. The main items are: 1) dangerous goods surcharge mapping to the correct revenue account, 2) reinforcing the minimum data set from operations, especially dates, and 3) clarifying how to handle claims in A3 and A2. All of these are already being addressed under T5, T12, T2, and T3. From an accounting perspective, I do not see any blockers that would prevent us from rolling out the new process, as long as we complete these fixes before go live.

I agree with that assessment. The issues in A7 are important but manageable. I would classify the dangerous goods surcharge mapping and the operations handover data as must fix before rollout, and the claims example updates in A2 and A3 as should fix but not blocking. Once the mapping and handover are corrected, the process should be stable enough for go live.

Based on the pilot results in A7 and the fixes already in progress for T5, T12, T2, and T3, I propose we proceed with a go decision for full rollout of the new relocation accounting process, on the condition that: 1) the dangerous goods surcharge mapping is corrected and tested, and 2) the operations handover template is updated and communicated. The claims guidance updates can follow shortly after without blocking go live.

threads.thread_goal: Prepare training, quick-reference materials, and audit evidence pack.

messages.text: With the pilot wrapping up, we need to finalise the quick reference posting guide and the audit evidence pack. I have shared a draft of the Bookkeeper Quick Reference Posting Guide as A6 and the External Audit Evidence Pack template as A8, covering T8, T9, T7, and T11. A6 summarises the main posting rules from A1 and A2, and A8 lists the standard reports and documents we expect to provide to auditors, aligned with A5. Please review and comment, and we also need to agree a time for the training session under T9.

A6 looks very helpful. I like the one page layout with common scenarios. For dangerous goods, could we add a short section that lists the extra steps: check job is flagged, confirm permits and certificates, use the dangerous goods surcharge and handling accounts, and update the dangerous goods log. That would tie A6 back to A5 and A2 clearly.

In A6, the section on claims and recoveries is a bit short. Since I got stuck on that during the pilot, could we add a simple example showing a small claim write off and a recovery, with which accounts to use and how to reflect it in the job costing template A3?

On A8, the list of documents for auditors looks reasonable: trial balance, relocation revenue and cost reports, dangerous goods log, and sample job files. I wonder if we should also include a copy of A2 and A4 in the pack, so auditors can see the procedures and the reconciliation checklist we follow.

Including A2 and A4 in A8 is a good idea. Auditors usually want to see both the procedures and evidence that we follow them. We should also reference A5 in A8, so they know how we interpret the statutory obligations for dangerous goods accounting.

For the training session under T9, I suggest a 60 minute slot covering: 1) overview of the new chart of accounts A1, 2) walk through of the SOP A2, 3) demo of the job costing template A3 and reconciliation checklist A4, and 4) review of A6 and A8. We can record the session for anyone who cannot attend live.
A 60 minute session works for me. If possible, could we include a short quiz or checklist at the end, so I can check if I have understood the main posting rules from A6?

I will expand the dangerous goods section in A6 to list the extra steps you mentioned and reference A5 and A2. That should make it easier to remember the sequence without re reading the full SOP each time.

Good point on claims. I will add a simple example in A6 showing a small claim write off and a recovery, with the correct relocation claims expense and insurance recovery accounts, and how to reflect them in A3. That should address the confusion from the pilot.

On A8, I would also include a sample of the dangerous goods log and one or two complete job files from the pilot, including A3, invoices, and supporting documents. That will show auditors how the process works in practice, not just on paper.

Agree. We should make sure A8 lists: trial balance, relocation revenue and cost reports, dangerous goods log, sample job costing templates A3, copies of A2, A4, and A6, and at least a couple of full job files from the pilot. That should cover most audit requests related to relocation.
For scheduling T9, how does tomorrow at 2 pm work for everyone? If that time is difficult, we can move to the morning, but we should keep it this week to stay on track for the 21 day go live.
Tomorrow at 2 pm works for me.
2 pm is fine on my side as well.
I can make 2 pm tomorrow.

To close on A6, the plan is: 1) keep it as a one page guide, 2) include sections on standard postings, dangerous goods steps, and claims and recoveries, 3) add references to A1, A2, A3, and A5 where needed, and 4) include a short checklist that we can also use at the end of the training session. Once I incorporate the feedback, we can treat A6 as final unless there are objections.

For A8, we will include: 1) trial balance and relocation segment reports, 2) relocation revenue and cost breakdowns, 3) dangerous goods log and related compliance checks from A5, 4) copies of A2, A4, and A6, and 5) a small set of complete job files from the pilot, including A3 and supporting documents. This should meet the external auditor expectations under T11. If there are no further additions, we can treat this as the final list for the audit evidence pack.
